thesis: Writing a book required the speaker to relearn structure, tolerate delayed feedback, and edit aggressively.
summary: The participant says his ease with short social posts did not transfer directly to a book. An editor rejected the initial approach, prompting a restart and work on storytelling. Unlike immediate online reactions, book writing involved months of uncertainty. He describes drafting chapters, cutting roughly a third, and selecting fewer stories to stay within length limits. The book commitment also overlapped a major acquisition. The interviewer's initial word-count description is inconsistent with the speaker's correction; this note treats the episode as a process account rather than relying on a precise abandoned-draft total.

insights.title: Learn the craft of a new format rather than assuming transfer
insights.explanation: The speaker expected to assemble familiar material but found book structure demanded different work. Editorial feedback changed the method rather than merely polishing sentences.
insights.quote: I thought it was going to be a combination of me um just putting together my my tweets That is not it
insights.speaker: unresolved

insights.title: Expect uncertainty when feedback arrives slowly
insights.explanation: The participant contrasts instant social feedback with months inside a manuscript. The observation explains his experience of doubt without establishing that such doubt measures quality.
insights.quote: When I'm writing a book I'm in my own mind for months on end
insights.speaker: unresolved

insights.title: Treat cutting as part of making the work useful
insights.explanation: The described process dedicates substantial time to shortening chapters and stories. The intended benefit is concise, actionable reading, rather than preserving every drafted word.
insights.quote: I would spend two days shrinking that chapter by about 30% word count
insights.speaker: unresolved

insights.title: Choose examples for the space and purpose available
insights.explanation: The speaker says 29 of 40 candidate stories made the book. This documents prioritization and permission or anonymity considerations, not proof that excluded stories lacked value.
insights.quote: I had to figure out which 11 stories were not as important
insights.speaker: unresolved
